name: StreamTok (Static Analysis for Efficient Streaming Tokenization)
workload: Streaming tokenization of JSON, CSV, TSV, XML, YAML, FASTA, DNS-zone, and log-file grammars, plus a worst-case synthetic grammar family (a{0,k}b)|a on a 10MB input, comparing StreamTok against flex-generated C lexers (and also nom/plex/regex in Rust, Reps' algorithm, and ExtOracle)
claimed_speedup: "a 2x to 3x speedup over existing tokenization tools such as flex"; on the worst-case synthetic grammar family, StreamTok has O(1) time-per-symbol vs flex's O(k) backtracking, so the gap grows unboundedly with grammar parameter k
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2640 v4 @ 2.40GHz / 128GB RAM (RQ1-RQ2 experiments); AMD EPYC 7252 8-core @ 3.10GHz / 256GB RAM (RQ3-RQ6, including the flex throughput comparison)
tradeoffs: StreamTok's O(1)-per-symbol streaming algorithm only applies to tokenization grammars with bounded 'maximum token neighbor distance' (max-TND); grammars with unbounded max-TND (the paper found this true for ~32% of a 2669-grammar GitHub-sourced sample, including grammars for C, R, and SQL) fall back to non-constant behavior. Requires a static pre-analysis pass and building a tokenization-extension DFA via powerset construction, plus a bounded lookahead buffer.
caveats: Peer-reviewed ASPLOS '26 paper (Li, Yang, Mamouras, Rice University) with a detailed reproducible-looking experimental section (hardware stated, multiple RQs, figures with real numbers), but I could not locate a public StreamTok source/artifact repository on GitHub, and the paper does not state Rust compiler version or build flags, so it is capped at Tier B rather than A. All numbers are read directly from the paper text/figures for RQ3 (Figs. 8-10); I did not independently recompute any ratios.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than flex" surfaced bojieli/ai-infra-book's mirrored conference-paper text for ASPLOS 2026 paper 152, "Static Analysis for Efficient Streaming Tokenization"

name: LRSTAR (DFA lexer generator)
workload: General lexer/scanner generation via compressed-matrix DFA tables, compared against flex-generated lexers and re2c-generated lexers, for compiler-style grammars with many keywords
claimed_speedup: "These are TWO TIMES the speed of 'flex' created lexers and about the same size"; separately, re2c-generated lexers are described as "up to 10% faster than DFA [LRSTAR] lexers", i.e. LRSTAR does not beat re2c
stars_or_usage: 0 stars on this GitHub mirror; author states the DFA lexer technique has been in use "since 1987"; original project hosted on SourceForge (sourceforge.net/projects/lrstar)
tradeoffs: Pure-DFA lexers can't natively handle matching-parenthesis-style constructs (author found a PDA-based approach ~5x slower and recommends handling that in the grammar instead); LRSTAR trades a bit of runtime speed vs re2c for much shorter lexer-generation (compile) time and smaller generated lexers, which matters for languages with large keyword sets.
caveats: First-party claim with a number but no stated compiler, flags, hardware, benchmark corpus, or linked benchmark code -- capped at Tier C. p7r0x7/LRSTAR is explicitly a third-party 'maintenance fork' of the original SourceForge LRSTAR project by Paul B Mann; the website page is copyright "All rights reserved" (2023), so despite source files being present in the repo there is no OSI license -- usability recorded as reference, not copyable.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "vs re2c" surfaced p7r0x7/LRSTAR website/dfa_doc_expert.html ("DFA vs flex" / "DFA vs re2c" sections)

name: CrossDB (hand-written SQL lexer/parser)
workload: SQL statement tokenizing and parsing inside an embedded/client-server relational database, using a hand-written scanner and hand-written recursive-descent parser instead of Flex/Bison-generated code
claimed_speedup: "a hand-written SQL parser that is over 10 times faster than Flex/Bison parser tools"; elsewhere: "approximately 10 times faster than Flex/Bison tools" and about one-third the code size of Flex/Bison-generated output
tradeoffs: Hand-written scanner+parser is harder to change than a Flex/Bison grammar if the SQL dialect needs to evolve, but the project reports it is smaller, fully reentrant/thread-safe, and gives better error messages than the generated alternative.
caveats: The 10x figure is an unsourced FAQ bullet point with no linked benchmark script, methodology, workload description, or breakdown between scanner-only and parser-only speedup, so it cannot be confirmed to isolate lexer/tokenizer performance specifically (it bundles scanning + parsing).
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "faster than flex" surfaced crossdb-org/docs docs/faq.md

name: Ragel State Machine Compiler
workload: examples/cppscan tokenizer benchmark implemented three ways -- Ragel, flex, and re2c -- and timed against each other in Ragel's own test suite
claimed_speedup: Ragel version "goes faster than flex version but not as fast as re2c version" -- directional claim only, no numeric ratio given
stars_or_usage: 239 stars on adrian-thurston/colm-suite (current home); 619 stars on the older, now-archived adrian-thurston/ragel mirror; widely referenced as a state-machine-based scanner generator (e.g. used to build Mongrel's/Cucumber's Gherkin parser, many network protocol parsers)
tradeoffs: Ragel embeds action code directly into generated state machines (goto-driven), which can outgrow flex's table-driven approach in speed but requires learning Ragel's own grammar/action-code language; project's original name/repo was folded into the broader Colm language suite.
caveats: Only a directional claim with no numbers, methodology, compiler flags, or hardware -- this is a Tier D entry (capped at one per run) included because Ragel is a long-standing, widely-referenced project, not because the flex claim itself is strong. The original adrian-thurston/ragel GitHub repo is archived; active development continues under adrian-thurston/colm-suite, which is used as the canonical URL here.
